newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Mkt to look past FOMC.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK - Mkt to look past FOMC.

text.p: With a practically bare economic data schedule and near unanimous agreement the Federal Reserve will keep rates steady, Wednesday will probably be the calm before the storm in the market.
It may even turn out to be a real yawner, as the market buys time ahead of Thursday's employment report for June.

"I think it is a range trade," said Patrick Dimick, Treasury market analyst at UBS Securities LLC, noting that the market did not even break out of recent ranges after a weakish purchasing managers report on Tuesday.

Normally when the Fed meets, the market's main focus is the results at around 1415 EDT/1815 GMT. But with virtually every trader, analyst and economist forecasting the Fed on hold, the Fed meeting is a non-event.
And, players said, when the Fed announcement declaring the end of the meeting hits, there will probably be no relief rally.
More important will be the minutes from the May Fed meeting, due on Thursday afternoon, market participants noted.
The market, they said, wants to know the Fed thinking on the spring slowdown and if it expects a summer rebound.
Meanwhile, traders said the market has little positioning to do ahead of the June employment report.

"We are stable going into employment," Dimick said, adding that accounts are neutral. Some expect a strong number and some weak, a contrast to a month ago when the market was all on the same side: anticipating a weak report.

A thin, pre-holiday environment could result in a wild ride Thursday. Data this week have been mixed. On Monday, some regional purchasing managers reported strong manufacturing in June. But Tuesday, the National Association of Purchasing Management said its overall index declined in June.
The drop in the NAPM index sparked a Treasuries rally that pushed up the 30-year bond 20/32 to 98-18/32. Its yield fell to 6.74 percent from 6.78.

At 1000 EDT on Wednesday, the Commerce Department releases its May factory orders report. Orders are expected to have fallen 0.1 percent in May, after a 1.2 percent rise in April, according to a Reuters poll of economists.
Traders said the market will likely ignore the report.
Garnering attention this week, players said, will be further release of June auto sales figures -- which began on Tuesday -- and chain store sales data on Thursday morning.
